prompt: Write an essay arguing whether schools should start later in the morning.
text:
# Why Schools Should Start Later

Every school morning, millions of teenagers drag themselves out of bed before their bodies are ready. Many start class at 7:30 or earlier. This is a quiet but real problem, and the evidence points to a clear fix: middle and high schools should start later in the morning.

## The biology of teenage sleep

Puberty changes the body's internal clock. Teenagers produce the sleep hormone melatonin later at night than children or adults do. A teen who is wide awake at 10 p.m. is not being lazy or stubborn. Their biology is working as designed.

Teens also need about eight to ten hours of sleep each night. If class starts at 7:30 a.m., a student must often wake at 6:00 or earlier. Falling asleep before 10 p.m. is hard for a teenage body, so many students fall short of the sleep they need. Over weeks and months, that shortfall adds up.

## What lost sleep costs students

Sleep-deprived students struggle to focus, remember lessons, and manage their emotions. Research on schools that moved their start times has found benefits in several areas. Students tend to get more sleep, show up to class more reliably, and report better moods. Some studies also find fewer car accidents among teen drivers, which matters because drowsy driving is dangerous for a group that already has little experience on the road.

Mental health is another concern. Chronic sleep loss is linked to depression and anxiety. Later start times will not solve those problems alone, but they remove one avoidable source of strain.

## The objections

Critics raise real concerns, and they deserve a fair answer.

**Transportation.** Many districts use the same buses for elementary, middle, and high schools, staggering the start times. Moving high school later means rearranging those routes, and that can cost money. But some districts have solved this by swapping the order, so younger children start earlier while teens start later. The cost is a one-time planning effort, not a permanent burden.

**After-school activities.** A later start means a later finish, which can crowd out sports, jobs, and family time. This is a genuine tradeoff. Schools can adjust by changing practice schedules, using lights for evening events, or shortening the gaps between classes. These changes take work, but they do not outweigh the benefits of well-rested students.

**Students will just stay up later.** Some worry that teens will simply shift their bedtimes and gain nothing. The research does not support this. When start times move later, students on average do sleep more, because their bodies keep the same late rhythm while the alarm moves back.

## A matter of priorities

Schools exist to help students learn and grow. A schedule that works against students' biology undermines that goal. Adjusting bus routes and sports calendars is difficult, but these are logistical problems with practical solutions. Chronic sleep loss in young people is a health problem with lasting effects.

Schools should not ask teenagers to fight their own biology every morning. Starting the school day later is a simple, evidence-backed change that supports better health, safety, and learning. Districts should make it happen.
